sections.title: Protected crops: shelter and control
paragraphs: Glasshouses and polythene tunnels admit light while creating a more controllable environment around a crop. Sunlight warms surfaces inside; the enclosure reduces the exchange of warmed air with the surroundings. Shelter also reduces wind damage and protects some crops from unsuitable outside weather. Heating, ventilation, irrigation and shading can extend the season or keep conditions within a useful range.

These changes can increase the harvested mass or number of usable fruits, leaves or other crop parts. Yield is not identical to the instantaneous rate of photosynthesis: successful flowering, fruit development, water supply and freedom from pests also matter. A tunnel does not automatically supply extra carbon dioxide or minerals, and it can overheat or develop high humidity if poorly managed.

example.question: Why might a tunnel improve a cold-sensitive crop, yet reduce yield on a very hot day?
steps: In cool conditions, shelter and warmer air can improve growth and extend the growing season.
On a hot day, inadequate ventilation can take temperature above the useful range and increase water stress.
A suitable answer links the controlled factor to this crop, rather than claiming that enclosure always helps.
example.explanation: This is a conditional biological explanation, not a prediction for every species or climate.

commonMistakes: A glasshouse does not make light, minerals or carbon dioxide unlimited.

sections.title: Carbon dioxide and temperature: separate limiting factors
paragraphs: Carbon dioxide is a reactant in photosynthesis. If its supply limits photosynthesis, enrichment can increase carbohydrate production and support more biomass and harvested yield. If light, water, mineral supply or another factor is limiting instead, adding carbon dioxide may have little effect. The enclosure can retain supplied gas, but ventilation to prevent overheating also allows it to escape.

Warming below the useful temperature range can increase enzyme-controlled reaction rates. Beyond a suitable range, enzyme function and other cell processes are impaired, respiration and water stress can increase, and yield can fall. The useful temperature depends on the crop and conditions; one universal optimum is not required. Light must be available for enrichment to improve photosynthesis: plants also respire in darkness.

example.question: Invented matched trials give 4.0 kg per plot without enrichment and 5.0 kg with enrichment in bright light. Under dim light, both treatments give 2.0 kg. Calculate the bright-light percentage increase and interpret the contrast.
steps: Increase = 5.0 − 4.0 = 1.0 kg per plot.
Percentage increase = 1.0 ÷ 4.0 × 100 = 25%.
No observed increase in the dim treatment is consistent with light limitation. Repeat independent plots and hold other conditions constant before a causal conclusion.
example.explanation: The values are assumed teaching data. They do not establish a recommended concentration, universal effect size or optimum temperature.

commonMistakes: More carbon dioxide cannot compensate for the complete absence of light.
Increasing temperature does not increase yield indefinitely.

sections.title: Fertiliser supplies minerals, not the plant’s energy
paragraphs: Harvesting crops removes mineral elements from the growing system. Fertilisers can replenish mineral ions that roots absorb. Nitrogen is needed to build amino acids and proteins; nitrate is one possible nitrogen source. Magnesium is part of chlorophyll. Relieving a mineral deficiency can support enzyme production, photosynthesis and growth, so more useful crop material is produced.

The plant obtains the carbon for most of its organic material from carbon dioxide through photosynthesis; light supplies the energy for that process. Mineral fertiliser is not a replacement for light or a store of food that roots eat. If minerals are already sufficient, extra fertiliser may not improve yield. Excess can damage roots through unsuitable conditions and can enter waterways, contributing to eutrophication.

example.question: A crop has sufficient water and light but is nitrogen-deficient. Link a suitable fertiliser to a possible increase in yield.
steps: An available nitrogen source is absorbed through the roots.
Nitrogen can be incorporated into amino acids and proteins, supporting growth and enzyme function.
More healthy plant material may develop; this does not show that every additional dose gives a larger yield.
example.explanation: Explain the missing resource and its biological use. Soil evidence and controlled comparisons matter more than the statement “fertiliser makes plants grow”.

commonMistakes: Fertiliser supplies mineral nutrients; photosynthesis supplies newly made organic food.

sections.title: Why control pests? Start with the damage
paragraphs: A pest is an organism causing an unwanted effect in a particular production setting. Insects may eat leaves or damage fruits, some transmit plant pathogens, and weeds compete with crops for light, water or minerals. Less functioning leaf area can reduce photosynthesis; damaged harvested parts may be unusable even if total plant mass changes little.

Identify the organism and the damage before choosing a control. Pollinators and predators can benefit a crop, so the mere presence of insects is not a reason to remove them all. Compare the likely loss with the effect, cost and non-target consequences of the proposed method. Chemical and biological methods can be combined if they do not undermine each other.

example.question: Explain why killing every insect in a flowering crop could reduce yield.
steps: Some insects transfer pollen, enabling fertilisation and fruit or seed development.
Others prey on crop pests.
Removing these beneficial organisms can reduce reproduction or allow pest numbers to recover.
example.explanation: The role of the species matters; “insect” is not synonymous with “pest”.

sections.title: Chemical pesticides: speed, resistance and side effects
paragraphs: A suitable pesticide can reduce a target pest quickly and can be applied across a production area. Its effectiveness depends on the target, timing, application and exposure. A broad-spectrum product may also harm pollinators or natural enemies; drift and persistent residues can affect other organisms. Persistence and food-chain accumulation are properties of some substances, not every pesticide.

Repeated use can select resistant pests. If inherited variants already tolerate the treatment better, they are more likely to survive and reproduce, making resistance more frequent. The pesticide does not cause each pest to deliberately adapt. Reapplication may be needed after new pests arrive, and a rapid initial reduction does not prove lasting control.

example.question: Invented starting population: 990 susceptible and 10 resistant pests. A treatment leaves 40 susceptible and all 10 resistant pests. Compare resistant percentages before and among survivors.
steps: Among survivors: 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%.
If resistance is inherited and survivors reproduce, its frequency can increase in later generations.
example.explanation: There is enrichment among survivors, not evidence that the treatment newly created the resistant variants. These are assumed counts.

commonMistakes: Not all pesticides persist or accumulate in food chains.
Chemical treatment selects resistance; it does not teach insects to resist.

sections.title: Biological control: choose a suitable natural enemy
paragraphs: Biological control uses another organism to reduce a pest population: for example, a suitable predator consumes it, or a parasitoid develops in or on it and harms it. An effective, well-matched natural enemy can reduce repeated chemical use and may continue reproducing while its prey is available. It need not eliminate every pest to protect the crop.

Control can be slower or inconsistent if temperature, humidity, prey availability or pesticide residues prevent the natural enemy from establishing. A species effective against one pest may not control another. Introducing an organism also needs attention to unintended effects on other species and habitats. Biological control is therefore not automatically harmless, free or permanent.

example.question: A predator reduces aphids in one protected crop but fails in another after a broad-spectrum spray. Give a possible explanation and a check.
steps: The spray may have killed or impaired the predator as well as the target pest.
Compare predator survival, residue exposure and pest counts with comparable untreated areas.
Different temperature or starting pest numbers are alternative explanations to control.
example.explanation: One observation supports a hypothesis, not certain attribution. A balanced comparison includes time, specificity, persistence, cost and non-target effects.

commonMistakes: A predator consumes prey; a parasitoid is not simply another word for predator.

sections.title: Yeast turns available sugars into gas that raises bread
paragraphs: Yeast is a unicellular fungus. During fermentation without relying on oxygen, it breaks down available sugars and releases energy for its cells, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide. At this course level the word equation is glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, with energy released. Flour starch must first be broken down to available sugars; do not describe the whole starch molecule as the direct substrate in that equation.

Carbon dioxide becomes trapped in the dough structure and enlarges gas spaces, raising the dough. During baking, heating expands gases, sets the bread structure and inactivates yeast; much of the ethanol leaves as vapour. Yeast can also respire aerobically when oxygen is available, so a freshly mixed dough is not necessarily completely oxygen-free. The anaerobic pathway explains its useful gas production as oxygen becomes limited.

example.question: Would adding ethanol alone reproduce the biological action of live yeast in a dough?
steps: Ethanol is a product of fermentation, not a living microorganism that generates carbon dioxide.
Live yeast metabolises available sugar and generates carbon dioxide that is retained in dough.
To explain rising, identify the gas and the dough structure trapping it.
example.explanation: Yeast does not photosynthesise, and oxygen is not the gas generated by this fermentation.

commonMistakes: Carbon dioxide raises the dough; ethanol is not the main raising gas.

sections.title: Plan a fair investigation of yeast under low-oxygen conditions
paragraphs: One possible investigation varies temperature and measures carbon dioxide collected from the same baker’s yeast and glucose mixture. A school method can reduce dissolved oxygen by using a teacher-prepared glucose solution that has been boiled and then cooled, with an approved thin oil layer to slow further oxygen entry at the liquid surface and the same small headspace in each vessel. Avoid shaking air back in. These precautions reduce oxygen availability; they do not prove that no oxygen remains. Carbon dioxide alone does not establish anaerobic respiration because yeast also releases it during aerobic respiration.

Allow the measured mixture to reach the chosen water-bath temperature before starting a fixed collection interval. Use equal viable yeast concentrations, sugar concentrations, liquid volumes, pH and collection arrangements. Gas volume per time is a proxy for activity under those conditions. A leak, blockage, dissolved gas or changing gas temperature can alter the reading without an equivalent change in metabolism.
commonMistakes: Bubble counts do not give gas volume if bubble sizes differ.
The highest measured value among a few temperatures is not proof of the exact optimum.

apparatus: Teacher-prepared baker’s yeast suspension, boiled-and-cooled glucose solutions and a suitable teacher-approved oil barrier
Suitable culture vessels and freely moving gas syringe with tubing
method: Agree the school risk-assessed method. Use a cooled, low-oxygen glucose solution, an approved surface oil barrier and equal small headspaces to reduce oxygen entry consistently. Do not boil a live yeast culture. This is a proposed investigation, not a completed trial.
Choose a range of temperatures within teacher-approved limits and verify the actual mixture temperature.
Equilibrate equal yeast and glucose mixtures for equal times; use fresh equal aliquots for every trial. Connect the gas collector and start a fixed interval consistently.
Record initial and final gas volumes and the actual temperature; never allow the outlet to become blocked.
Repeat with independent preparations at each temperature. Include a comparable no-yeast blank to check non-biological volume changes.
Keep collected gas at a comparable measurement temperature, check leaks and account for any non-zero blank before comparing rates. Investigate anomalies rather than deleting them automatically.
variables: Independent: temperature of the yeast mixture.
Dependent: carbon dioxide volume collected per unit time.
Controlled: viable yeast concentration, sugar concentration, pH, total volume, equilibration/collection time and oxygen conditions.
safety: Teacher supervision and school risk assessment apply. Use safe water-bath temperatures, eye protection and prepared suspensions; avoid inhaling dried yeast.
Keep electrical equipment and hands dry, secure glassware and keep gas outlets unblocked; never seal a rigid vessel against accumulating gas.
Do not taste experimental mixtures; clean hands and surfaces and dispose of cultures through the school procedure.
quality: No performed trials are claimed. Residual headspace/dissolved oxygen and the oil barrier’s effect on gas release need checking; do not infer strict anaerobic conditions from carbon dioxide alone.
Repeat variability estimates precision, not proof of absence of systematic error.
Check gas-temperature expansion and collection losses; carbon dioxide can dissolve in the mixture.
A sugar-concentration comparison is another option, but change one factor at a time while controlling the rest.

sections.title: Interpret repeated gas readings without inventing an optimum
paragraphs: Subtract the initial gas volume from the final volume before dividing by the elapsed time. Calculate a mean from independent repeats, while retaining the raw readings and noting unusual values. A mean collected-gas rate is a measurement of this setup, not a direct count of dividing yeast or an exact total energy-release rate.

Compare rates only if yeast amount, measurement duration, collection efficiency and gas measurement conditions are comparable. More samples around an apparent peak would help locate a maximum for this strain and substrate. A fall at a high tested temperature may be consistent with impaired enzymes, but a failed gas seal is a different possibility that the controls should investigate.

example.question: Invented five-minute gas-volume increases: at 20°C, 12,14,13 cm³; at 30°C, 21,23,22 cm³; at 40°C, 10,12,11 cm³. Calculate each mean rate. Assume the blanks are zero and collection conditions comparable.
steps: 20°C mean = 39 ÷ 3 = 13 cm³; rate = 13 ÷ 5 = 2.6 cm³/min.
30°C mean = 66 ÷ 3 = 22 cm³; rate = 22 ÷ 5 = 4.4 cm³/min.
40°C mean = 33 ÷ 3 = 11 cm³; rate = 11 ÷ 5 = 2.2 cm³/min.
30°C gives the highest measured mean here; intermediate temperatures were not tested.
example.explanation: These are invented observations, not a performed experiment or a universal optimum. The rate unit includes time; a mean volume alone is not a rate.

commonMistakes: Equal bubble counts can conceal different total gas volumes.
Agreement between repeats does not exclude a shared leak or calibration error.

sections.title: Lactobacillus acidifies milk in yoghurt production
paragraphs: Suitable lactic acid bacteria, including Lactobacillus, metabolise milk sugar and produce lactic acid. Falling pH changes the interactions of milk proteins, especially casein, helping form the thicker yoghurt structure. The acid also contributes to the sour taste. This is different from yeast producing ethanol and carbon dioxide to raise dough.

Production uses a selected starter culture and controlled conditions. Heating the milk before inoculation reduces unwanted microbes and also affects its proteins; the milk is cooled to a suitable culture temperature before the starter is added. The starter must not be killed by adding it to excessively hot milk. Cooling later slows further microbial activity. This explanation is not a home food-safety recipe, and acidity does not guarantee that every contaminant is absent.

example.question: In an assumed culture, pH falls from 6.5 to 4.6 and the milk thickens. Explain a plausible biological sequence and one limit of the evidence.
steps: Starter bacteria metabolise milk sugar and produce lactic acid.
The lower pH helps casein proteins aggregate into the yoghurt structure.
The observations are consistent with that process, but pH alone cannot identify the species or prove the product is safe to eat.
example.explanation: The pH difference is not a percentage change in acidity: pH is a logarithmic scale.

sections.title: Industrial cultures: keep competitors out and resources available
paragraphs: An industrial fermenter is a vessel used to grow a selected microorganism under controlled conditions and obtain cells or useful products. Unwanted organisms can consume nutrients, spoil a product or introduce harmful substances. Aseptic precautions reduce contamination: equipment and medium are sterilised appropriately, inputs are protected and a known culture is introduced without adding unwanted organisms.

Sterilising the system happens before growing the intended culture; continuing to kill all organisms would also kill that culture. A nutrient medium supplies substrates and mineral resources suited to the organism, supporting respiration, synthesis and reproduction. Nutrient depletion or waste accumulation can restrict growth even when temperature is suitable. The harvested material may require separation and purification rather than being usable straight from the vessel.

example.question: Why would sterilising a vessel and supplying nutrients still fail if contaminants entered with the incoming air?
steps: The unprotected air could reintroduce competing or harmful microorganisms.
These can consume nutrients or change the product and growth conditions.
Protect inputs, for example with a suitable filter in an aerobic system; asepsis is maintained throughout the process.
example.explanation: A clean start alone does not prove that the culture stays uncontaminated.

sections.title: Temperature and pH require monitoring and correction
paragraphs: Microbial metabolism releases heat, so a large active culture may become too warm even if the room temperature is stable. A temperature probe monitors the culture, and a controlled jacket can remove heat or supply it when required. Below the suitable range reactions may be slow; excessively high temperatures can impair proteins and cell function. The target is specific to the organism and production process.

Metabolism can also change pH. A pH probe and controlled adjustment keep acidity in a useful range for enzymes and growth. A probe measures a condition; it does not correct it by itself. Temperature control cannot replace pH control, and neither guarantees unlimited growth or maximum product yield if other resources are exhausted.

example.question: Explain why a cooling jacket is useful even when warm conditions favour the organism.
steps: Respiration and other metabolism release heat inside the culture.
If heat accumulates, the culture may exceed its useful temperature range.
Removing surplus heat maintains suitable conditions rather than making the culture as cold as possible.
example.explanation: Connect the device, the controlled variable and its biological consequence.

sections.title: Aeration and mixing solve different problems
paragraphs: For an aerobic production process, a suitable oxygen supply supports aerobic respiration. Filtered air can be delivered into the culture. An agitator distributes organisms, nutrients, dissolved oxygen and heat, reducing local shortages or hot regions. Introducing air without mixing does not guarantee equal conditions throughout a large vessel.

The required oxygen conditions depend on the microorganism and intended process. In industry, “fermentation” can refer broadly to cultivation in a fermenter, including aerobic processes; it is not a claim that every industrial culture respires anaerobically. Anaerobic products need appropriate low-oxygen conditions instead. Excessive agitation or aeration can also damage some cultures or create foaming, so more is not always better.

example.question: A process needs oxygen. Explain why a stirrer and an air inlet are both useful.
steps: Air supplies oxygen that the aerobic culture can use in respiration.
Stirring distributes that oxygen and nutrients through the culture and reduces uneven temperature.
The inlet supplies a resource; the stirrer helps distribute it.
example.explanation: This is a functional explanation, not an instruction to oxygenate every microbial process.

commonMistakes: Industrial fermentation is not synonymous with oxygen-free metabolism.

diagram.alt: Original functional diagram of an aerobic culture vessel: protected nutrients, filtered air, mixing, temperature and pH monitoring, cooling and a sample or harvest outlet.
diagram.caption: Original functional model for an aerobic process. Sensors inform control; targets depend on the organism. Not a universal operating specification.

sections.title: Fish farming: oxygen and waste are linked
paragraphs: Fish farming can supply dietary protein by rearing fish under managed conditions. Fish need suitable water quality, including dissolved oxygen, temperature and chemical conditions for their species and stage. Oxygen supports aerobic respiration. Aeration and water circulation can help, but the whole balance matters: fish, microbes and other organisms use oxygen, and warmer water can hold less dissolved oxygen under otherwise comparable conditions.

Faeces, metabolic waste and uneaten food accumulate unless managed. Decomposition of organic matter can raise oxygen demand; nitrogenous waste can harm fish if it builds up in unsuitable forms or concentrations. Systems may remove solids, exchange or treat water, and manage biological filtration where appropriate. Clean-looking water is not proof of adequate dissolved oxygen or absence of harmful dissolved waste.

example.question: Why can excess uneaten feed reduce fish growth rather than improve it?
steps: Uneaten organic matter becomes substrate for decomposers.
Their aerobic respiration can increase oxygen demand, while waste and dissolved nitrogen compounds may accumulate.
Poor water conditions stress fish and can restrict respiration and growth.
example.explanation: Follow feed through a biological mechanism; do not treat water appearance as a complete quality test.

commonMistakes: A biological filter converts some wastes; it does not make maintenance or oxygen supply unnecessary.

sections.title: Predation and disease: manage distinct sources of loss
paragraphs: Intraspecific predation is one fish eating another of the same species; interspecific predation involves different species. In a cannibalistic species, separating markedly different size groups can reduce loss of smaller fish. Screens, suitable enclosures or protective netting can reduce access by outside predators such as other fish or birds. Competing for food is competition, not automatically predation.

Crowding and poor water conditions can favour disease transmission or stress. Checking stock health, separating new or affected groups where appropriate, hygiene and suitable stocking levels help reduce risk. Treatment depends on identifying the problem; adding an unspecified chemical is not an explanation of disease control. Measures have to fit the species and farming system and still allow water exchange, feeding and welfare.

example.question: A large fish eats a smaller fish of the same species; a bird eats another farmed fish. Classify each and suggest a physical control.
steps: The same-species event is intraspecific predation; size grading may reduce it in a cannibalistic stock.
The bird event is interspecific predation; suitable protective netting may reduce access.
Assess the control without assuming that every fish species is cannibalistic or every enclosure excludes every predator.
example.explanation: Use the species relationship, not simply the difference in size.

sections.title: Feed quality, timing and inherited traits affect production
paragraphs: Feed must supply suitable nutrients for the species and growth stage. Amount and frequency should match stock biomass, feeding behaviour and conditions: inadequate feeding restricts growth, while surplus can waste resources and worsen water quality. Distributing feed helps reduce unequal access. A fixed amount per fish is not appropriate for all sizes or all stages.

Selective breeding uses parents with desirable inherited characteristics, such as growth performance or disease resistance, and selects suitable offspring for later breeding. Repeating selection can change the stock over generations; extra feeding changes conditions for current fish and is not itself selective breeding. Reduced genetic diversity or linked undesirable traits can be disadvantages. Any measured difference in growth also needs comparable rearing conditions.

example.question: Invented comparison: stock A receives 80 kg of dry feed and gains 50 kg of wet fish biomass; stock B receives 90 kg and gains 50 kg. Calculate dry feed per kg of biomass gain, assuming comparable survival and accounting.
steps: A: 80 ÷ 50 = 1.6 kg dry feed per kg wet biomass gain.
B: 90 ÷ 50 = 1.8 kg dry feed per kg wet biomass gain.
A uses less supplied feed per recorded gain in this comparison. Differences in waste, survival, starting stock or environment must be checked before attributing this to inherited traits.
example.explanation: This assumed ratio is not a trophic energy-transfer efficiency: dry feed and wet fish mass have different water contents. It is not a prescribed feeding schedule.

commonMistakes: Giving more food is not genetic selection.
A mass feed ratio does not directly measure energy-transfer efficiency.
